distress-tolerance/accepts.note: ACCEPTS's "Activities" category draws on the same prepared list.
Both are multi-tool distraction toolkits for surviving the moment — learn both, choose one per situation.
ACCEPTS resets the mind by distraction where TIPP resets the body — choose by whether the crisis feels somatic or cognitive.
After surfing the peak, distraction (ACCEPTS) can carry you the rest of the way down.

distress-tolerance/actions-based-on-valu.note: Values clarify which alternative behavior is worth the cost of change.
Once you accept what you can't change, channel the freed energy into a value-based proactive plan.
Once the body is calmer, re-engage with what matters instead of the urge.
Willingness opens you to effective action; your values point to which action.
The long-term part draws its goals from the Actions Based on Values worksheet.

distress-tolerance/cost-benefit-analysis.note: Later, when calm, analyze whether the crisis behavior you spotted here is worth changing.
After the crisis passes, if it was driven by a recurring behavior, analyze it while calm to prevent the next one.

distress-tolerance/distracting-activitie.note: Grounding turns attention toward present sensory reality; distraction turns it away toward an activity.
When the warning sign is an urge to act, buy time by distracting away from it.
The "Engage in a distracting activity" step draws directly on your prepared distraction list.
Both are gentle activity-based routes through distress; soothing calms via the senses, distraction shifts focus.

distress-tolerance/grounding.note: Both are quiet, low-effort, present-moment ways to settle without physiological intervention.
Cognitive spiral (not bodily arousal) calls for reorienting to the present.
Both work through the senses — grounding reorients to the present, self-soothing adds comforting sensory input.

distress-tolerance/half-smile.note: Half Smile is the body-based way to practice non-resistance while you accept.
A gentler body-based option when full TIPP is too much or unavailable.
Soften the body with a half smile while you ride the wave.

distress-tolerance/radical-acceptance.note: Use ACCEPTS until intensity decreases, then shift to Radical Acceptance.
Accept what you can't change, then invest the freed energy in what you value.
The body-calm of a half smile opens the door to accepting what you can't change.
Once the urge is handled, move from surviving toward accepting what you cannot change.
You radically accept the facts first; willingness is the flexible stance you then take toward them.
The source links Radical Acceptance as the companion stance.
Accept the fixed part, then work on your thoughts and responses as the source suggests.
The source points to Radical Acceptance for guilt or shame after owning a mistake.
The source points to Radical Acceptance when mutual respect is absent and can't be built.

distress-tolerance/recognize-emotional-c.note: Feed the crisis behaviors you identified there in as the behavior to analyze here.

distress-tolerance/resistt.note: Both are multi-tool distraction toolkits for surviving the moment — pick one per situation.
This prepared list is the raw material for RESISTT's "Engage in a distracting activity" step.
When very activated, use active distraction (RESISTT) first, then self-soothe as intensity drops.

distress-tolerance/self-soothing.note: Both are gentle activity-based ways through distress; self-soothing targets the senses to calm, distraction shifts focus.
Both calm through the senses — grounding reorients to present reality, self-soothing adds pleasant sensory comfort.

distress-tolerance/tipp.note: TIPP is a momentary rescue; values-based action is the long game that reduces how often crises arise.
TIPP is fast and in-the-moment; this is slow and deliberative — choose by whether you are calm enough to think.
Grounding reorients attention without the physiological jolt of TIPP — a gentler route when the body isn't in full alarm.
Acute bodily arousal is the signal for the fastest body-based down-regulation.
TIPP jolts the body to down-regulate fast; self-soothing gently comforts — choose by how intense the arousal is.
A cold-temperature jolt (TIPP's ice cube) can steady you while you surf a strong urge.
TIPP is the body-brake when STOP's step back and breaths aren't enough.

distress-tolerance/urge-surfing.note: ACCEPTS distracts away from the wave; urge surfing rides it — opposite mechanisms for the same urge.
This decides a behavior is not worth it; urge surfing is how you ride out the urge without acting on it.
Distraction moves attention away from the urge; urge surfing stays with it — opposite strategies for the same urge.
Soften the body with a half smile while you ride out an urge.
RESISTT manages the urge by shifting away from it; urge surfing sits with it — opposite mechanisms.
Urge Surfing rides out an urge; exposure rides out the emotion behind it. Same wave-like logic.
Riding out the urge is a way to stop feeding the habit this page flags.

distress-tolerance/willingness-vs-willfu.note: Willingness is the open stance; your values supply the direction to act in.
You must accept the facts before you can willingly, flexibly work with them.

emotion-regulation/abc-please.note: This is ABC PLEASE's Build mastery letter worked out as a goal plan.
Coping ahead is the C in ABC.
PLEASE covers the same body-care areas as a memorable acronym.
The source recommends lowering emotional intensity with ABC PLEASE first.

emotion-regulation/balancing-emotional-u.note: Acting opposite to the urge to isolate or avoid gets the first task done.
The source's example rehearses opposite action for social anxiety.
Exposure holds still and lets the emotion pass; opposite action does the reverse of what it urges. Choose by whether staying still or acting differently fits.
Opposite action is the practical counter to that belief.
You need to see the urge before you can judge whether it's effective and act opposite.

emotion-regulation/being-effective.note: Turns Build mastery into concrete short- and long-term goal steps.

emotion-regulation/coping-ahead.note: The full rehearsal procedure behind the C letter.
The source's Coping Ahead example rehearses opposite action before a feared event.
Coping Ahead rehearses the solution you choose here.

emotion-regulation/emotion-exposure.note: Opposite action changes what you do; exposure changes nothing and waits the emotion out.
The source links exposure as the practice for myths that emotions must be avoided or acted on.
Allowing an emotion is the stance exposure asks you to hold for five minutes.

emotion-regulation/emotions-cognitive-vu.note: The companion page on thought patterns; body and mind are the two sides of vulnerability.

emotion-regulation/emotions-physical-vul.note: The longer page on diet, sleep, exercise, stress, and addiction covers PLEASE in more depth.
The companion page on the body; thoughts and physical state are the two sides of vulnerability.

emotion-regulation/myths-emotions.note: Examine the myth behind the judgment so it stops recurring.

emotion-regulation/problem-solving.note: Problem Solving picks the response; Coping Ahead rehearses it.
Problem Solving's brainstorming step asks you to reframe exactly these distortions.
Problem Solving opens with the same behavior analysis of trigger, emotion, and thoughts.

emotion-regulation/recognizing-your-emot.note: You need to name the emotion and its urge before you can choose the opposite.
Step one's behavior analysis is the same trigger-emotion-thought breakdown.
That analysis shows the secondary emotions; self-validation is how you stop adding them.

emotion-regulation/self-validation.note: Myths like "feelings are weakness" are what self-validation pushes against in the moment.
Self-validation targets the harsh secondary emotions this analysis exposes.

emotion-regulation/stop.note: STOP buys the pause needed to check whether the urge is effective.
The source recommends pausing with STOP, then using wise mind, to tell honesty from reactivity.
The source advises grounding with STOP first; GIVE works better when your nervous system is settled.
Pause and step back before re-engaging.

interpersonal-effectiveness/assertivenes.note: The scripts supply the "I think / I feel / I want" phrasing this page recommends over "You are...".
An "I feel..." statement is a ready way to voice the hard truth the honesty step asks for.

interpersonal-effectiveness/barriers-to-.note: The "old patterns" barrier is these passive and aggressive styles carried over from upbringing and past relationships.

interpersonal-effectiveness/communicatio.note: The "old patterns" barrier is the passive and aggressive styles described there.

interpersonal-effectiveness/dear-man.note: For a dreaded conversation, the skill to rehearse is often a DEAR MAN script.
The "I feel" and "I want" scripts are ready phrasing for DEAR MAN's Express and Assert steps.
DEAR MAN pursues the objective; FAST makes sure you don't trade away self-respect to get it.
The source frames GIVE against DEAR MAN; DEAR MAN leads with assertiveness, GIVE with kindness and connection.
DEAR MAN structures the direct statement of a boundary.
Set the intensity first, then deliver the request with DEAR MAN.
Repeating your point is DEAR MAN's "broken record" under the Mindful letter.
DEAR MAN packs the same describe, express, ask, negotiate sequence into a memorable acronym.

interpersonal-effectiveness/fast.note: The rights to decline without guilt and set boundaries are what FAST's No apologies rests on.
FAST targets the habit of giving up self-respect to keep the peace.
FAST keeps your self-respect intact while DEAR MAN pursues the objective.
The source pairs GIVE with FAST to hold a boundary calmly when the other person is rude or aggressive.
FAST keeps you from apologizing for or abandoning a boundary under pressure.
FAST's "Stick to your values" and "No apologies" carry this page's refusal and values skills into the moment.
FAST's Truthful letter is the honesty step applied when you're standing up for yourself.

interpersonal-effectiveness/give.note: If the trigger is a person, proceed mindfully into the conversation with GIVE.
GIVE keeps the delivery warm; together they get the request and keep the relationship.
FAST protects your self-respect; GIVE protects the relationship. Lead with the one that matters more here.
GIVE's Interested and Validate letters are these listening and validation skills in compact form.
A gentler presentation is what GIVE provides.
These skills hold your position against pushback; GIVE softens delivery to protect the relationship. Choose by which matters more right now.

interpersonal-effectiveness/interpersona.note: The source lists assertive boundary-setting among the alternatives.
The right to set boundaries is put into practice on the boundaries page.
Saying no assertively is boundary-setting in action.
Deciding who has earned your honesty is the same reciprocal judgment as opening your boundaries.

interpersonal-effectiveness/listening-an.note: The same validation, turned toward another person.
Interested and Validate are the listening and validation skills in compact form.
Skill one applies validation to someone who is resisting you.
Getting information relies on the same genuine questions and curiosity listening practices.
The understanding-and-respect step uses reflecting the other person's view without judgment.

interpersonal-effectiveness/modulating-i.note: Weigh urgency against their vulnerability before setting the Assert step's strength.

interpersonal-effectiveness/resistance-a.note: Resistance skills keep the exchange going when a well-phrased statement meets opposition.
Validating their view and asking for specifics extend the Mindful and Negotiate steps.
Validating the other person's view is the first resistance skill.

interpersonal-effectiveness/skills-of-as.note: Part 1's "know your priorities" step is the remedy for the identifying-needs barrier.
Knowing your default style shows what assertiveness has to replace.
Assertiveness voices your side; listening and validation acknowledges theirs. Effective communication needs both.
Calibrates how strongly to ask once you know what you're asking for.
Completes the six-skill framework that Part 1 starts.
Saying no without damaging the relationship is the most common boundary in practice.
Part 2 completes the six-skill sequence with getting information, saying no, and acting on values.

interpersonal-effectiveness/trust-in-rel.note: Opening boundaries to people who trust you with theirs goes hand in hand with judging who has earned your trust.
Reflecting someone's view without judgment is how trust's "understanding and respect" step is practiced.

mindfulness/describe-your-emotions.note: Describing emotions names the feeling; this page widens the lens to context, interpretation, urges, and outcomes.
The acknowledging step is naming the emotion plainly, without judgment.
Once you notice internal events, describing your emotions names the strongest of them.
Noting surfaces emotions in passing; Describe Your Emotions examines one of them in depth.
Tracks the emotion each judgment produces — the same emotion-clarity skill from M4.
Uses emotion-naming as its emotion-mind input, then weighs it against the facts.

mindfulness/internal-vs-external-events.note: Sharpens the internal-awareness half of M3 into naming one specific emotion.
Scanning the body is internal-event awareness — the inward half M3 balances against external focus.
Observing is the base attention skill M3 turns inward and outward to balance.
Balancing internal and external awareness is the same integration Wise Mind formalizes for decisions.

mindfulness/letting-go.note: The non-judgmental "I am thinking/feeling..." phrasing is the same move Letting Go uses to reframe a judgment.
You must first catch automatic judgments before Letting Go can reframe them — this is the pair's first half.
Both create distance from sticky thoughts — defusion by imagery, Letting Go by reframing a judgment.

mindfulness/mental-body-scan.note: The body scan is a focused way to practice the internal-awareness half of this exercise.
Two body-based calming practices; pair breath focus with a body scan.
Observing a single object first builds the attention control you then move across the whole body.

mindfulness/mental-noting.note: Mental noting labels emotions in passing; describing goes deep into one emotion's action and thoughts.
The rewrite uses mental noting's "I am thinking/feeling..." phrasing to strip judgment from a thought.
A targeted form of mental noting aimed specifically at judgment thoughts.
Observing anchors on one external object; mental noting tracks the moving stream of thoughts instead.
Extends mental noting — after noting a thought, imagery lets it drift away, loosening its hold.

mindfulness/mindful-breathing.note: The page's remedy for overwhelming emotions is noticing body signs and mindful diaphragmatic breathing.
Both relax through the body; the scan opens with settling breaths and shares the same calming aim.
The breath is a portable object of observation — use it when no object is at hand.
Steady breathing is the ground from which you watch thoughts pass instead of chasing them.
Opens with the settling abdominal breath from Mindful Breathing before examining the problem.

mindfulness/mindfulness-of-negative-judg.note: All-or-nothing self-labels are the automatic judgments that page teaches you to catch.
Takes the judgments M9 taught you to notice and reframes them into non-judgmental observation.

mindfulness/observing.note: Grounding is applied Observing; practicing Observing when calm makes it easier to notice when you need to ground.
Sitting with the emotion is nonjudgmental observation aimed at a feeling and its body sensations.
The O step is nonjudgmental observing applied mid-reaction.
Applies the observing stance to two arenas at once — inner experience and the outer environment.
Rewrite judgments as if observing the situation from outside — the objective stance from Observing.
The body scan extends single-object observing to sensations across the whole body.
Turns the observing stance inward, onto the passing stream of thoughts and feelings.
Observing applied to the breath — a single, always-available object of attention.

mindfulness/thought-defusion.note: This page disputes a distorted thought; defusion steps back from it without arguing. Choose by whether the thought responds to evidence.
Another way to loosen a sticky judgment — defusion drifts it away, Letting Go rewrites it.
Noting a thought as a thought is the base Thought Defusion extends into actively creating distance from it.
Steady breathing is the ground from which you watch and release thoughts.

mindfulness/wise-mind.note: Once you're a few notches calmer, move to a Wise Mind check-in.
Use Wise Mind when you're unsure what the proactive next step should be.

Consult Wise Mind to check that the willing solution you've chosen actually feels right.
The source recommends evaluating each belief from wise mind.
Proceeding mindfully asks what wise mind would choose.

Finding your priorities starts from wise mind, observing your feelings to see what's missing.

Wise Mind opens with abdominal breathing to settle the mind before deciding.
